chapter: Pittsburgh school days and old jealousies
title: Slavery stories, hitting her teacher, and the Pittsburgh school
summary: Overhearing her great-grandparents' slavery tales so angered her that she hit teacher Miss Itzel. She argues children should hear the whole history of black America.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: What really happened - I used to hide under the bed. I don't know if I told you about this and I think it's a terrible thing that anybody would indoctrinate a black kid against what happened to them when they were in slavery, what happened to their parents when they were in slavery, because it affected me so when I was quite young. I was in the third grade, I remember. I usedto hide under the bed and listen to my great-grandparents talk about slaves and things. It infuriated me so that when I went to school I hit my teacher, Miss Itzel, with a stick. I just walked in school and hit her with a stick.

I said, "You hate black people and I hate white people," something like that. So Miss Itzel said, "This poor child," and she bought me dolls and candy and everything and Miss Milholland heard about it. They discovered I had perfect pitch and she did everything about instruments and a lot of things - she's so talented she can play all the instruments. She had a music store to send all the instruments out to me and I played violin and the teacher got rid of me fast. He says to them, "You better not bother her because already she's playing "The Sheik" on one string." You just leave her alone and let her find out her own music and find out what she's going to do." As I said before, Miss Milholland would book me over for afternoon teas at
the Tech University and other little gigs. That's the reason why I think it's very bad in telling a child about anything that has happened in the past against any race of people.
In your case it wasn't the school that was telling you this, this was overheard in your home?

This was overheard. You see, my great-grandparents were born I guess about a year after the slaves were freed. They were both very fair, my grandmother especially. My grandfather had blonde hair. She used to tell how they used to put them out in the sun and try to parch them black because they were very, very fair and my grandmother is too. I'd hear them tell all these tales and about the slaves and what had happened. It really angered me and I can understand what's happened to the young black kids of today, because they really shouldn't - they should find out the history but they shouldn't hear too many things because they start thinking wrong. But eventually
When you say they shouldn't hear about the history, you mean they should get the whole -
The whole and not just pieces of it.
And especially they should get the history of black Americans. I think that's really what they need now.
You say the school was a white school that you went to?
Yes, it was an all white school.
